original_value: Recent interest in ethical AI has brought a slew of values, including fairness, into conversations about technology design. Research in the area of algorithmic fairness tends to be rooted in questions of distribution that can be subject to precise formalism and technical implementation. We seek to expand this conversation to include the experiences of people subject to algorithmic classification and decision-making. By examining tweets about the "Twitter algorithm" we consider the wide range of concerns and desires Twitter users express. We find a concern with fairness (narrowly construed) is present, particularly in the ways users complain that the platform enacts a political bias against conservatives. However, we find another important category of concern, evident in attempts to exert control over the algorithm. Twitter users who seek control do so for a variety of reasons, many well justified. We argue for the need for better and clearer definitions of what constitutes legitimate and illegitimate control over algorithmic processes and to consider support for users who wish to enact their own collective choices.

result.paraphrase: Growing interest in ethical AI has brought values such as fairness into discussions of technology design. Work on algorithmic fairness is typically grounded in distributional questions that can be formally specified and technically implemented. We aim to broaden this discussion to include the experiences of people who are classified and judged by algorithms. Looking at tweets about the “Twitter algorithm,” we examine the broad range of concerns and desires expressed by Twitter users. We find that concern with fairness, in a narrow sense, does appear, especially in complaints that the platform shows political bias against conservatives. But we also identify another major category of concern, seen in efforts to gain control over the algorithm. Users seek such control for many reasons, often with good justification. We argue for clearer and better definitions of legitimate versus illegitimate control over algorithmic processes, as well as support for users who want to carry out their own collective choices.
